segments.words: Well you know I was here about Summerfield and... Summerfield, Jordan, Moody. Moody used to go out, especially in the lumberjack country, and act like a whole lumberjack. Makes them buy some and then they...

segments.speaker: George Mckeever
segments.words: Glom right onto them, you bet. Throw them in the jug. I could tell you one very good story about a moonshine, but I don't think it...

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: You just don't use any name. Don't use any name.

segments.speaker: George Mckeever
segments.words: When did we have real tough times? What was the year? 19 when the banks went broke? I had a patient come in, he wanted some uppers and lures… dentures… and I knew what he did. He lived way back in the brush and he made the darn stuff and pedaled it. Five dollars a gallon is what he got for it and he made good moonshine. Corn liquor. And he was to be picked and pay me as soon as he sold us the next batch. The revenuers got him. His wife came in here, went in, bragged him in this room. He went, they had you wait until everybody left and I said, I'm not going to say her first name or better not. And I couldn't... I don't... I was going to say his first name. You know, my husband's got that stuff out there in the hills and we've got a WPA force of guys working on the road between here and there. And they know if I come downtown here with that darn stuff in there, they'll know what I've got under the hay in this old wagon with two horses on it.

segments.speaker: George Mckeever
segments.words: And he said, do you do something for me? I said, what do you want me to do? Take your car and come meet me way up there in the brush… and I did… i wanted my money for the work I did. They had this stuff all sold. I went up there and I met this lady and everybody was waving at me when I went past this WPA crew… what was it?

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: It was the WPA.

segments.speaker: George Mckeever
segments.words: Right… we never offered what they're picking, so we didn't know. They had no machinery. I had to do it all by hand, you know. I went out there and I got 13 gallon jugs and put in the trunk of my car. And I come sailing back down through there and about, maybe at the time she got there it'd be two hours later, you know, coming to get her groceries. And the bed was all flat and the hay piled up and so she sailed right through and nobody talked about it. I brought that stuff down, run my car in the garage and that night, they knew their customers and that night the next morning it was all gone. And I got my money. ...That's true. Yes. And he is dead and his wife just lives over the hill and she still, and I see her in town occasionally, why she still, once in a while she will mention that, you know. My gosh, the roads were terrible, you know. I didn't know whether I could even get my car back through there and go through a big one or a very husky one. It was a jute. You can remember back that far. I've seen the pictures of it. And it was an old jute two door outfit.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Just that curiosity, were they from the south?

segments.speaker: George Mckeever
segments.words: No, born and raised right here. Yeah.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Because, you know, a lot of people were really outstanding moonshiners that come from those, the hills.

segments.speaker: George Mckeever
segments.words: Back in the Kentucky and back in the Ozarks. Because we made a trip down through there one time. Up in the sticks room, it was really rustic, you know. We got right into it back there. You've seen pictures of these three old tall skinny guys, you know, these funny cartoons. And there the men were sitting on the porch barefoot and feet sticking up on the railing around the rim of a mountain garden home with great big man's eyes hoe as you know. No clothes, lines of clothes after wash day were hanging on the bushes around drying instead of having hound dogs all over the place. And I was going by real slow so we could get the full view of our whole situation. And one of those home dogs, they had, I must have had 20 of them, plume dogs. And they all come troppin' across the road right in front of me and I stopped. Started up and one dog turned right around to go back, run right over. I tell you brother, I give a full steam ahead. I never stopped. I didn't want one of those old lads to get that old squaw gun out and take a pop at me. Back in the Ozarks. My folks all came from back in Missouri, Kansas City, Lee Summit. And we'd been back there on our way down to New Orleans. We went all the way around the whole United States on that trip. My oldest girl got out of the university, my youngest girl got out of high school. And that was their graduation present. We went all the way down the west coast, around the whole bit and up in the Missouri and then the CR folks. And then back down to New Orleans and over into Florida and up the east coast to New York and on Boston. And then back through Chicago home. Had a little boat to the picture, I remember that.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did you have to give credit a lot in those days when it was kind of rough?

segments.speaker: George Mckeever
segments.words: I have taken in everything when I first started to work. Money was mighty scarce. You bet. Potatoes and meat and what have you. Vegetables, chickens, fryers, bring in a dozen ... I'd back my car out of the garage and when I have a butchering mess out there in the garage, all four of us would work, you know, Ruby and Paula and Chloe and myself. I'd chop their heads off, we had hot water, we scalded them. By the time they got to the end they were ready to be cut up and wrapped and put in the deep freeze. Take a dozen fryers at a time. Good chickens, not the kind you buy, but they sit on wire cages and the meat is all flabby. These were chickens that run in the barnyards and the meat had a entirely different flavor to them than these chickens we buy in the supermarkets today. Because they just sit on those wire cages and get fat and they butcher them.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did you find that you could trust almost everybody?

segments.speaker: George Mckeever
segments.words: No problem… once in a while you'd run into a stinker, but it might be one year, it might be two years, and it might be five years. But it's not like today, you know. Now they take bankruptcy or do anything under the sun. Not so much recently, but a few years ago that was a big way to get into the end and then take bankruptcy and beat you… you bet.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did you notice a big change when the Depression hit in people's ability to pay for the work?

segments.speaker: George Mckeever
segments.words: Nobody had any money. I think when the banks went broke, Roosevelt shut them up and then they were shut for some time. I think they had $3 .45 in my pocket and that was all. What little bit of head in the bank, you couldn't touch it… and we lived… we ate just as good as we ever did. That's what you can do in a farming community. You couldn't do that in a big city. When I first got out of dental college, Ruby says, okay, we'll go back. I'll stay five years and then really if you know how many years has been.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: She said she'll stay five years?

segments.speaker: George Mckeever
segments.words: She says five years, remember moving out of a small town.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: That's God's truth, right? Did she change her mind?

segments.speaker: George Mckeever
segments.words: Sure she did, yeah. She'd always lived in a big city. Always had, all her life. Except when she came down here, around that ranch in Cashup, you know, where Robert's in.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: She'd go to his farm and every time he'd go to Spokane, see that house over there?

segments.speaker: George Mckeever
segments.words: Next to the old Robert's ranch. That's where she'd spend some vacation time out there, you know. She found that small town life was... It wasn't too good. It wasn't too bad… right… get your feet on the ground. I can go out and dig around in my yard. It'll kill me to go to a city where I didn't have a yard. In the last few years we've talked what in heaven's name are we going to do in these few lots I've got in my far beds. What are we going to do? Cooped up in some little 12 by 12 apartment room and go to some retirement home where there's nuts. This is a beautiful place to be retired just as well as the lawn. Yes. When we get a little odor and a little ... and not able to do our chores, you know, get out in the yard or mow the lawn, it's pretty hard to get somebody to come and help you. I have this one lad across the street who is... and he will work for me, but these old kids, they've all got money. They've got cars.

segments.speaker: George Mckeever
segments.words: Who wants to go out and mow your lawn? They can make $20 a day or $30 a day or whatever they make. Working for a farmer or hauling grain trucks or working in the woods. Do you know what they get a day working in the woods… fantastic… six and seven dollars an hour. Who wants to mow a lawn… yeah… they're not bashful. Here we have hunting, we have fishing. We have big game hunting. I used to go every fall, get my elk and my deer. The hills are getting steeper now than they used to be. And I haven't gone hunting for a long time, but I still go fishing with my buddy. Rhonda's dad. And we go back up to Locksaw. I haven't been at the Locksaw for three years because of Ruby's need. She doesn't... she can't... she has me down.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: We talked to her grandfather when he was still living, Henry Yes. You know, one thing I wanted to ask you about is about oral hygiene in those days. What I'm wondering about is how people took care of their teeth.

segments.speaker: George Mckeever
segments.words: Do you know what they did in those days? They never had the money to buy as many cakes and pies and cookies as they do now. They didn't have the sugar content in their food. They had better Oscar teeth. They had more roughage to chew. They didn't make a difference whether they brushed their teeth or not. But the food that they ate, coarser bread, kept their teeth clean. The king wasn't as prevalent as it is now.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: It's funny, I would have guessed it would have been worse then.

segments.speaker: George Mckeever
segments.words: No, no. It was the coarser grain of food that we ate.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did they brush?

segments.speaker: George Mckeever
segments.words: No… very seldom… very seldom… and now they've all got to do it, you know. They used dental floss and all this, but they never did before. When I first started in, 57 years ago. That's really something. I imagine that the teeth would be a lot worse because they wouldn't be, you know, using toothbrushes, toothpaste and all that stuff. Yeah. I know. You're just... The farmers, they never, they ate. They raised what they ate. And that they didn't have the soft foods that we have today. Prepared breakfast cereals. Take a look in the grocery stores at the many, many different kinds of cereals for the kids, you know. And all the vitamins are cooked out of them and all the good stuff is gone after they go through this heat process of making them, you know.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: I hear over and over again people, especially those that live out in the country, say, I never saw a doctor, you know, until I was 30. My mother never saw a doctor until she was 80 and broke her arm. And it makes me wonder, were people reluctant to come to you?

segments.speaker: George Mckeever
segments.words: They were healthier… and when they got sick, they were really sick and they died. They died young. What if they had a ruptured appendix? He had a rising..… remember that word… a rising. Not a swelling. He'd have a tumor, a ruptured appendix or something, take the bucket. He was dead and that was all of us too. They buried him. Now the good national, Spokane, or most of them, or Moscow, or to where there's a clinic. And the good care, you know, now. They don't wait. Yeah, there's a lot of difference in the way the people live in those days than they do today.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What about teeth? Would they let their teeth go a lot longer if they had a problem than they would today?

segments.speaker: George Mckeever
segments.words: The main thing was, if anybody ever knew, let it decay and that went along far enough, that was extracted. There was no bridge work done. That came along after we had Roosevelt. A lot different than it was then. But still, the methods are the same.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did you have an novocaine then?

segments.speaker: George Mckeever
segments.words: But I'll tell you something funny about that. We bought our novocaine in little glass bottles, a hundred little pills in a bottle. And then we had distilled water. We had a little porcelain container that would hold maybe two cc's of water, distilled water. And we'd heat that over an alcohol flame. Drop your one pill in, or if you wanted four cc's, drop in two pills. And you made your darned novocaine and then sucked it up into an old type of syringe. And you're ready to inject. It took longer to get ready than it does now for a person to come in and sit down and have a tooth anesthetized and extracted and you're out and gone. And then when this new system came out where they made the little cartridges, and you opened your syringe and shot that thing in there and you were ready for business. You buy the little glass cartridges, we call them, by the seal in, just like a can of coffee or something. You break the seal. You can hear the air, you know, come in or go out, whichever it does. And there you've got a fifty in a can of sterile solution. And you can just put it in and put your hand in there, your own hypodermic needle in there and you're in business.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Were people more affected or less affected by pain in those days?

segments.speaker: George Mckeever
segments.words: By far. I've taken the teeth out of a person many times, no again aesthetic at all. And that was it. Don't you touch me with that needle, just pull that damn tooth. Yeah, that's a fact.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What about the women?

segments.speaker: George Mckeever
segments.words: That's what I'm talking about. There's one woman I had in mind and she lived right down across the bridge here. I better not talk about this. I could show you the house. The house is still there where she lived. And in the early days when we had three big saloons here in town, where's a picture of the flood? And I'll tell you that. And that is a real story. I'll tell you about that one… okay… can you see a white house right there… now that's where the lady was that I had in mind that I told you about. Pull them out, pull them out. And I pulled every one, 26 of them, I can remember. And she just brought a little and I pulled a whole darn smear. But that house where she lived in, now way back in the early days,… i don't know whether to say it or not, but it's God's truth, it's history. The Red Light District was right in that house. And when we had the flood, us damn kids would go down there and watch the business fair and get in the boat. And go across to that place. And there's the house and that's where she lived in. And that house still stands. Right.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Well every town of any size had one.

segments.speaker: George Mckeever
segments.words: No, but I'm showing you where this one is. ... The businessmen, or whoever, had to take out a rowboat to go out there. I'd rather dance.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: That's um, when someone had to have older teeth pulled at once, like that lady, that'd mean that she'd been living with pretty decayed teeth for a while.

segments.speaker: George Mckeever
segments.words: As a rule. Some of them, their diet possibly wasn't as good as it should have been. And then the gums would go out on them. So a lot of them had ... So they would have ..., you know. And it was much different in those days. After you removed all their teeth, go on home and come back in six months. And they went around the same with no teeth for that long. Their mouth would all shrink out of shape. And then you had to put in a couple of bundle racks when the dentures were put in. Took them forever to get used to them. And now you know where you pulled the last two and put the pick right in… bundle racks.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What were the dentures like then?

segments.speaker: George Mckeever
segments.words: Old black rubber… black rubber… this will give you an idea. We had two kinds of denture material rubber. And I burnt those and took the teeth out just to show people what it was like, you know. And then we got something a little better. This is thinner, lighter, and better grade of rubber. And that's what they are. And here's what they have to be.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Could people, would most people wear them?

segments.speaker: George Mckeever
segments.words: Oh yes… they wear them. They very seldom would...

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What about, let me ask you a little bit about style in those days. I mean you looked at a lot of people's faces and, you know, I, like, when I look at these pictures, all these old men that had beards, a lot of facial hair, and they're not quite completely out of style. What do you think, why the difference? I often wondered why that thing. What was it, was this, I mean people must have felt comfortable with wearing their hair.

segments.speaker: George Mckeever
segments.words: Here's a picture taken right after the flood. And if you know the town at all, here's where the Methodist Church is up there now. And old Bobby Burns had his photographer's office there in the bottom, and you can see here where he displayed his work. And he lived up topside. And here is the debris still in Main Street. You can see the dirt and the logs and the ark and one thing or another. And here is several old, I don't know what, they got pack horses and every turn, every one of those got a mustache. So that was the style in those days. And they finally got away from it. My dad wore a mustache when we were little kids. And after a while he cut it off and he never grew another one after that. I think it's just the way, what would you call it, time changes, people have different ideas. You see full beards now. Coming back. Yes.

segments.speaker: George Mckeever
segments.words: And we are all a little different. I wouldn't be caught dead with anything on, no I wouldn't. I had a kidney taken out last fall up and I got hurt in an African safari. I got bruised pretty bad and Rhonda got her knee hurt. But that's beside the point. But I had lost a kidney up in St. Pete Deaconess Hospital last October. And I just couldn't wait until I was there to let me come to enough so I could get my face shaved. What terrible. I shave every day of my life, Sundays, holidays, it don't make a bit of difference. Every day I shave. And I about went nuts up there for those three or four days after surgery before I could wobble out of my, off that bed and get across the room. You bet. So you see we are all different.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Well I was, I'm always struck by that, all that, all those beards. Yes. And then the long dresses of the women, the way they dress. Yeah.

segments.speaker: George Mckeever
segments.words: Let me get down here in personal history now. This is my mother's family. And I'll bet you this picture was taken in March the 16th, 1901. Now there's, here there's my granddad. And you see some of the old men from here. Here's my own father, seeing how the birth is. And here I am sitting down here, this is taken back into the room. That big family's there… show him his… mother had five brothers and one sister. So you see he was a Quaker. Not a Quaker, a friend. Which is an offset, like Mennonites or what have you. And a friend was an offset of some Quaker, I don't know what, a little ranch of the Quaker tribe. And he always ate apple pie for breakfast, first thing in the morning. Had to have his apple pie before he ever had cereal or ham and eggs or whatever. I thought that was his dad's name.

segments.speaker: George Mckeever
segments.words: My mother's father… a carpenter, a cabinet maker… 1853… other stock. I've never kept a similar set of them. And then a total, here's another total. Now he worked. And over here is his daily labor for that year. He got $266 .50. He worked a hundred and about 13 days. The amount was $266. He got $235. I bet he bought a Cadillac. Now, and the price of the wool in the hobs and the heifer cap. And then his daily wage over here. He made $500 and $8 .25 that year. Now I'm going to show you an envelope that I'll bet you might have, but I doubt. Postmaster here, he put this away from me. This is a letter addressed to my granddaddy. Right for post office, Union County, Ohio. The guy says he paid three cents. They did or not. Then after he got to write in the letter, he folded it up to make the envelope. And I want to show you how he addressed his parents. And here's the date.

segments.speaker: George Mckeever
segments.words: Third month of fifteenth day, in 1852. Respect and Relation. Said a hi dad, hi mother. Or brother, or whatever. I don't like to open this thing up in too much, but I wondered how. I wondered how he, here's wishing friends.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What do you mean… your well-wishing friends.

segments.speaker: George Mckeever
segments.words: What have they heard? I don't know. That's how my, here's granddad I know. But respect and relation. And the postmaster here, I showed this to him. Anybody had a fit? It's beautiful. He wanted to get it away from me. And I said, you go jump in the letter. After I'm dead, he'll go have it I suppose. And then I had another one. This guy's brother was a sharpshooter in the Civil War. And that letter was that thick. History knocked you down to read that letter. And I give it to my oldest daughter when she was here last to take it home. I'm sure. Husband, Don San Diego. Here's another old timer. And it's pretty badly worn out. 1855. Uh-huh. But look at the handwriting and the long-term thing. It's probably so close.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Yes, yes. You can still just make it out.

segments.speaker: George Mckeever
segments.words: The three words in that diary that the social sharpshooter used, was just as plain as that yearbook. Beautiful writing. They don't do it anymore. No. I got a grandson that can't read his damn writing. Absolutely. He's 20, 22 years old. The kind of scratching you ever saw. When I went to school, we hadn't spent Syrian or something. I don't know why. But gosh, we only practiced that and rubbed up and down on our hands. Every day we had exercises in writing. When I was in school, I came to the pictures I showed you. Classes, you know.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: You know, one thing I had heard that you had a lot of Indian patients.

segments.speaker: George Mckeever
segments.words: When I first came, I could really speak Nez Perce. My dad was a fluent speaker with the language. Because he worked in a hardware store, and those darn Indians from Lapwai and all down in there would come up here for their training. So he got off to his old old toxic allowance and his old brother really jabbed. I had hundreds of Indian patients.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Because of him?

segments.speaker: George Mckeever
segments.words: No, because I was close to them. But now, public health service, and it's all free, and you and I pay for it. And they got a wonderful dental office in Lapwai, down there on the reservation, you know.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: But in the 20s, many of them came up to me.

segments.speaker: George Mckeever
segments.words: I had hundreds of them. Half Indians out here, you know.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What were they like?

segments.speaker: George Mckeever
segments.words: Indians, women all wore shawls, the women and the men both all wore moccasins… you bet… you don't see it anymore. Until now you see an old squaw with moccasins on, with these younger generations, gosh. They're just like these hippies, you know, now, whatever you want to call them. Dressed right up to snuff, you know.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did they speak English?

segments.speaker: George Mckeever
segments.words: Oh, yes. Yeah. I never had a problem. Because I talked to them and said, I have nothing to you. But, hey, what's this in Nez Perce? And they tell me, every time one would come in for this morning, I'd read them in Nez Perce. If it was the afternoon, you'd read them a little different, you know. That's ... in the afternoon. Good afternoon. Not in ..., good morning. So, I've forgotten it. Ever since this, yea, who came in down here, who is part Indian? And it's alright, that's a good deal. And when we got it, they never paid me. They bought the requisition from the agency. And I filled in my bill and sent it, and six months later, I got my check from the Empire Colorado… yeah.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did they come only for real essential work?

segments.speaker: George Mckeever
segments.words: Oh, the old, the, when I first started fifty years ago, then the older people then, you know what I mean by that, my old patients had fifty years ago, you know. Then they would only need the extraction or even dentures. But the younger people, they had their bridges made and their partial plates and what have you, same as you and I would now name her. You would, not me.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Well, you know, one thing that I've wondered about them, that I'd like to find out more about is that, in a lot of places, they really weren't welcome. You'd take Lewiston and other places, they couldn't even go in, a lot of places.

segments.speaker: George Mckeever
segments.words: I never put the set the dog on any of the door, it was open if they wanted to come to me, fine, I took care of them. And treated them just the same as if I would treat the white person. No, hanky, hanky about it at all. The bill was the same for those folks as it was for anybody else, although I sent my bill in the agency, they always went to the agency and brought this requisition sheet with them. And once in a while I'd get in a hurry and the girl that was told, gee, she was a pretty Indian gal, she would call me on the phone, I'd send him to him, so he's in trouble, take care of him and I'll name you the requisition, you know. She's even a beautiful Indian lady girl, young girl, just good luck… boom… no wonder some of those guys went nuts? Well, I was thinking of the way that Indians acted on their part, did they, did they, did you have a feeling that they were, um, I had the idea that they really kind of cut off white people to some extent, at least they do now. I wonder if they were outgoing and friendly or rather reserved when you kind of...

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: No, to me, I wanted to speak for myself, but to me they were just as friendly and just like you and I talk. They'd all gone to a school down there in Lapwai, they had good teachers, some of them talked. I had the Haskell University graduates here from down here at Lapwai, that would be the order, you know, be old, intelligent, speak better English than I ever could, yes. Because my wife gives me hell yet because I don't use proper English. But you talk to some of these lumberjacks and a little of it grubs off on you. And I goof a little bit and then she burns my ears for me, you know. Yeah, that's not... She's pretty strict on English and I wasn't very good ever in English, even in high school or any time. The hell with it, it didn't... that was a small part to me and still is. If I can tell somebody what I want or explain something to me, that's good enough. But not so to Ruby, it's got to be just... She reads a lot, man, I'm telling her, she's out of this world.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What about the Ku Klux Klan in the 20s? They were active in most of the towns around here.

segments.speaker: George Mckeever
segments.words: Never have I ever seen a Ku Klux in a white... nightgown, I burned my life in this town, there are no meetings.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: No crosses burned?

segments.speaker: George Mckeever
segments.words: No crosses burned, and I'm not here. Maybe someplace else, maybe Lewiston or Moscow. If so, I don't know, it's out… nothing… now, maybe they had them, but I never heard of them, if they did. There was a short life in the 20s, and I think most of these towns did. I never knew of one here in Kendrick that ever was… i never did… sometimes people have told me they had pocket cards, you know, like a credit card or something that you did belong to. It looked a few k's, but I never saw one. I just never asked, and I never went to any of the meetings. Nothing. Kind of stupid, huh?

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: I've tried to figure out what they were doing, because it didn't seem like there weren't hardly any reason that I could figure why there would be.

segments.speaker: George Mckeever
segments.words: You saw the picture of The Birth of a Nation, and the old Griffith put on quite a show there for four hours. And that's how it started when those fellas scared the pants off of those little nigger boys with these white sheets. And that was all in fun, but it took a whole ton from there it grew. But, never around here. Not to my knowledge. All I did was work in my garden and go to Masonic Lodge, school board meetings. And send to Councilman.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: You know, there was it, now I had heard there was one fellow that got arrested for moonshine, and now it was him. Well, I heard it was a professional man around here. I had heard first he was a doctor, and then somebody said he was a vet, or retired vet.

segments.speaker: George Mckeever
segments.words: You're talking about my old buddy. He was a paper hanger. He was a painter. He had gone to school two years at some vet school back in the Kansas City or someplace back there. And run out of money, and then he came west. And I can take you out here and show you where he had his house, his home. And he had his office in there, and his tools in an old traveling bag, you know. And he did lots of veterinary work. And one time he'd come by and he says, come and go with me. I'm not, you know what? We talked about floating horses teeth. I said, what do you mean, Van? What do you mean by floating horses teeth? They had a big old file on a handle iron handle that long, and they'd wear a horse would wear a tooth, so it was a sharp point on it. And would either cut their cheek or their tongue. And they would quit eating. And the farmers would call him in, and he'd come up in the thickies, put that bridle in to force the mouth open. And he'd come up, and he took me with him one day. And he used to stick your hand back in and feel that. He'd put my arm back that far in that horse's mouth, and that thing was just like a needle. Now he said, I'll go to work. And he took that with both hands, and he just, just like an old wood rest. And he'd just rest that old enamel down, just like going crazy, you know.

segments.speaker: George Mckeever
segments.words: And I said, Van, don't that hurt? Wait till I get home, I'll show you. The nerve in that horse's tooth was down that far. There was no pain to that at all. He said, that horse never batted an eye, and it wasn't an ... or a thing. He said, forget that old stuff. Van worked, you bet. He lived right here, his son. His son got off on the wrong track. We took Freddie in our house, and he did everything under the sun, I guess. From his dad moonshining, from that to drugs. And he went to New Wilson, got in with a Chinaman in the majestic cafe, and he was a regular hop head. And we drove Van, sent Freddie down to our place, and let us receive what we can do for him. I kept Freddie here all month summer. And he even bought him an old runabout car that was in pretty good shape, and got him in as a lookout in the Forest Service. And from there, he never did quit the drugs. He finally committed suicide in Grangeville. And I went to his funeral. And old Van worked.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What happened to how he did get caught?

segments.speaker: George Mckeever
segments.words: You mean the father, looking like her? He would come to town and get pretty drunk and talk too much. A peep is drunk every day in his life. The old gentleman, you know, the veterinary, the two-year veterinary man, he should have gone another year to school, but he graduated at that time. And I started a year sooner than I did. I would have graduated in three years. I was among the first of the class that only had to go four years. And now he equals six. So there you are. Big difference, you know.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: So you think the fact that he didn't graduate, now that meant he couldn't really practice, he couldn't be a regular vet?

segments.speaker: George Mckeever
segments.words: He did not have a state license. No. What he did, we called it bushwhacking. Outside the law. But he did a lot of work here. Saved a lot of horses and a lot of cows, a lot of animals. You're mad that he knew. But liquor got the best of him in mind. He drunk it and then I belly-goat it… every day… ...

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: He didn't have a wife there?

segments.speaker: George Mckeever
segments.words: I never knew her. She was dead. He had two children, a boy and a girl.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: So there wasn't anything to hold a boy back?

segments.speaker: George Mckeever
segments.words: No… they lived pretty crude.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: I've heard that Hophead, so that was a problem back then too. That it wasn't, there really was that going on. Where would something get started on something like that in those days?

segments.speaker: George Mckeever
segments.words: Well, I remember that'd be a hard question for me to answer. How would that kid get from here to those, to no car and get in with somebody that was a Hophead and then he got introduced to the Chinamans in the ... affairs, still in business. But it's a different group of people running it. And there's where Fred got the boy. Right up in that bedroom up there, he'd take his shot. My wife would set up with him a half a night talking to him. And he was such a good kid, likable kid, and worked like the devil.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: I guess I read that you could almost, like you could get a legal prescription in the drugstores for something that was like it, was addictive in some way or other before without law. That's what I, before it was made illegal.

segments.speaker: George Mckeever
segments.words: Lordy, 75 years ago, my mother had a bottle of laudanum in the kitchen up in the, what would you call it, for the dishes or caused? And whenever we ate some green apples or some darn thing and got the belly ache, she would count laudanum out. And laudanum comes from opium. And you could buy it in the drugstore here, just like you go in and buy it, it does nags. And she'd count out so many drops of that in a tablespoon full of water. And we'd drink it, and sure, it was an archive. It stopped the belly ache, and that just kept going out on the plate, and that was all it was. But that bottle was up in the cupboard for a hundred years, it seems to me like, until we grew up, until it was outlawed… laudanum.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did you ever hear about Psychiana and Frank Robinson's redemption in policy?

segments.speaker: George Mckeever
segments.words: what was the name of that automobile? ... No, no, no, no, no. He had great big exhaust pipes sticking out on the hood, you know, and running way back. Oh, yes, I knew the old rascal, you know, and he had that Psychiana. And he had people working for him, he had money coming in from all over the world. When I was going to university in Moscow, and that was going on. Some little kids would go downtown, and we stayed at a, this is good for you. So, now I'm poor, we were, it was pitiful. And about 30, 37 of us guys got together. And we rented the house and hired a cook, and the cook had two daughters. We paid them at the house rent, and we paid her, we took care of our own rooms. And we brought our laundry home for that, and the most I ever paid was twelve dollars a month for board and room. And that's when old Robinson was going around with that fancy sport automobile, you know, that tailpipe going down on the outside of the car, you know. But, aluminum looked to me like chrome, chrome possibly. And, yes, old Robinson was up there then. And Moscow was named after him. Right, he donated that to him.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did you ever have any idea about the sincerity, his sincerity, whether he really believed, or what he was, that's a general impression, I've heard.

segments.speaker: George Mckeever
segments.words: This guy from India kind of fell in love with this junk that he was writing. Now that I said junk, maybe I'm wrong. He got a check for thirty thousand dollars from this kid who was up there in school, from this one Indian print from India. That was common knowledge up there when I was going to school. Yeah, I had heard something about that before. I read some of this stuff not too long ago, trying to understand better what he was doing. I never read any of it. I told you junk, and I took it back because I don't know, it might have been just a number one.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: He was involved, he got quite a tiff with the editor of the publisher, the other Moscow paper.

segments.speaker: George Mckeever
segments.words: The Star?

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: The Star Media. That was the old Lamphere. I guess Lamphere was, at least he, Robinson said it was Lamphere behind this, but you know they tried to deport him. They had that big trial up there. I went back and read the old papers over there right at that time. Interesting, interesting situation.

segments.speaker: George Mckeever
segments.words: We never knew what's getting in school. I worked in the chem lab up there for research professor at the University over in old Marl Hall. From school I'd go over there at night and work, and I brought more money home the next spring when I had my money in, and that's what I took to school. Every bill had to be in the first month. Then when he got the bills all in, he called us all in. Here's what we paid out, you owe us so much, and we gave him five dollars a month for keeping the books.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Boy, that sounds like a good way to go to go to school...

segments.speaker: George Mckeever
segments.words: Right, but we called it just a co-op, and they had these co-op clubs up there at the University, or did a few years ago, maybe not now.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: You called it a co-op then?

segments.speaker: George Mckeever
segments.words: No, we just called it our house. We didn't have sense enough to call it a co-op. I'll bet the co-op name wasn't even in existence, probably. I don't know, we didn't call it that. I had my oldest daughter graduate up here, and the youngest one was here now from Boise visiting us, and she just called me to tell me that she was eating lunch with one of her old school friends. Both girls graduated from the University of Idaho many years ago. Those girls, 50, the youngest one was 46.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did you mind not being in a fraternity when you were there?

segments.speaker: George Mckeever
segments.words: I couldn't afford it if I did, so I never thought of it… that was how… remember the Kappa Sigma house? Those big columns up in front? Us kids would walk down from the ad building, and the guys would be out there beating on the banjo or something. That must be a pretty good life. That's about all we ever said. They have enough money to live in a deal like that and be able to pay for the... pay for your board. ... It had to be, because we didn't have any money. Nobody had any money in our place.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: When you think about the way most families were in those days, do you think that most of them were poor?

segments.speaker: George Mckeever
segments.words: Yes.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: In their early days?

segments.speaker: George Mckeever
segments.words: Right… you're a darn right, they were. They made a living. My dad worked for $50 a month here in that hardware store. And $50 a month, by the heck, of a lot longer now than several hundred dollars will go… we'd bet… get some of these old newspapers and read the ads what the price of different articles were, you know, like when N. B. Longs came here and started the store in 1908. And once in a while, Marvin will tell about how much it cost when you start first in the store, you know. Absolutely could have hoped that. Eggs, maybe. Just a few cents a dozen. And we almost had a oot meal for breakfast. Always. All of my life. Cooked cereal. We never heard of post-toasties and all this old bunch of crap, you know, they have now. We bought it in a 10-pound white, like a flour sack. A 10-pound sack. And we almost had cereal for breakfast. Always had bacon and eggs, ham and eggs. Or sausage and eggs. And mother was from the south and we always, all my life, we had a hot biscuits every morning.

segments.speaker: George Mckeever
segments.words: Right… hot biscuits every morning, mother can have a batch of hot biscuits on the table in three minutes. That'd be better if you can. ... You started. Right. In an old wood stove. ... Every morning after me. For a lifetime. From a youngster back in the East Summit, Missouri. And we and I have been back there on the old home place. And it was sold to this unity. I don't know whether you've ever heard of it or not. The headquarters for unity is on my mother's ranch out of Kansas City. It's known the world over. Unity Village. And that's all it is. Unity Village, Missouri. And that's on their envelopes. So it's known the world over, you know. And they have ministers from every denomination. Catholics, Baptists. Anything you might want to call. They go there for steady periods. Seminars. So it's got to be a pretty broad... broad...

segments.speaker: George Mckeever
segments.words: You name it… right, yes.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: When you talk about your mother then, do you feel that women worked very hard?

segments.speaker: George Mckeever
segments.words: My mother was a slave… you bet… room and I have talked about it many times. What did she do? How did she spend the day? A kid came into town after he got big enough. Came into town two miles to school. What did mother do? Dad came to town early. He had to be at work at seven o 'clock here in town and walked in two miles after breakfast. What did mother do during the day? She had chickens to feed. She had her chores, her bread to make. Pies and cakes and stuff like that. And she... Old... we had rag carpets. Now, day after day after day she would spend tearing pieces of material into strips that wide and then sewing them together. When those kids come home from school we'd wrap them in balls. And the balls would be almost the size of a basketball. And there was no lady here in town that had a weaving machine which you got a hand weaver with the shuttles that I've washed her. And she would make a carpet out of those rags that mother would sew in and us kids would roll them up and be balls. So every room was carpeted but it was rag carpets. And we thought we were something. Nobody else had rag carpets. But that's one thing mother did to spend her time during the day. We came home at four. School at nose time started at nine o 'clock in the morning. We let out at twelve. We went back to school at one and we were out at four. And we cut the hell out of there and went home to get our chores done. We had cows to milk and chickens to help feed and then corn to shut for the hogs and milk the cows and take care of the horses and what have you. Even out there on two miles from here.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Would your mother have been working the whole day?

segments.speaker: George Mckeever
segments.words: Be busy in the house doing her chores baking bread and making butter making preserves canning fruit. She was the busiest preparing woman here myself. She never had. She never read. I had one magazine in my life to read at home when we were kids. Youth's companion. It came once a month. And we had those folksmen review twice a week. And that was all the reading we had. We had no libraries. We had no library books. We had no novels to read. It was important enough to your family to live out of town for you for you kids growing up. To keep us kids out from running with the rut of rag muffins here in town. That their dads were in the saloons drinking beer and the dad didn't want that. We had a bottle of whiskey up in the cupboard. A pint of whiskey and that was there year after year after year. If we had a cold he had a hot pot in him at the bed. Nobody ever drank any liquor in our family.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Never. So that was the main reason he wanted you to wait for the bad influences in the town.

segments.speaker: George Mckeever
segments.words: Correct and keep us busy. Instead of loafing around and fighting and getting in trouble.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: So he kept some stock and you had farm work to do.

segments.speaker: George Mckeever
segments.words: Right. We had in the summer and the summer vacations we had wood burning stoves. And at Christmas time my dad would hire some man to come out and he would fall down pine trees. And then next summer we would haul them into the wood shed. 12-14 cords maybe. And that would last us in the cook stove and the heating stove in the living room for a whole year. We never had time to get in trouble. Every other Saturday we got to go fishing. And that was great.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Now does that mean that you were working most of the time when you were in school when you were a kid?

segments.speaker: George Mckeever
segments.words: Darn right we worked. Everybody worked. But I mean now the difference, the relative work to play. You know what I mean.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: I mean how much of your time was work? Was it mostly working? Can you tell me what the heck two boys and a younger sister could do for play? What would they do? Two guys couldn't do anything could they? Can you tell me a name?

segments.speaker: George Mckeever
segments.words: Mumblety-Peg. And at noon sit out in the shade of the house and play mumble pig with a jet knife. We didn't have marbles. We were too poor to have marbles. Yes but I never had marbles when we were kids… no… now we were busy. We cut the hay with a mower. We had a rake and we raked the hay… two horses… the hillside was so damn steep we couldn't use a wagon. We had quite a long sled. We could haul in enormous loads on that sled down that hill you know because it was... And after we went over that bunch of grass you know it would get pretty slick. Those old ponies would have to go pretty fast to keep Adams. No break. Just go to the hill. We'd stash it up in the barn. Had an old Swede come and help us one time and put up hay. And we had a quite large barn with a driveway through the center. And he would stay on the sled and he'd pitch the hay up to me on the landing and then I'd pitch it on up to my brother. He'd go back in the corners. And that old Swede run the pitchfork through me one time. Right there's a scar yet. He'd run it in here and it came out here and he just pulled it right over and tore it out. And I screamed and I yelled and the blood was running down. And I jumped from where that landing was down on the haylaid load.

segments.speaker: George Mckeever
segments.words: Where in the hell do you think you're going? I'm going to the house. You heard me. Let me see. And he took a big chaw to back out of his mouth and slapped her on there and he reached around in my hip pocket and got an old red bandana handkerchief. He wrapped it around there and tied it. Get the hell back up there. And I went back to work. I'm not lying to you. I'm Mrs. Agachtruz. And you can still see that dang scar for you. You know. At least darn roses. But you can see part of the scar right there yet. Can you see it?

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Yeah, I sure can.

segments.speaker: George Mckeever
segments.words: He stabbed me. Charlie Carson was a guy's name. And he came out to help us get the last bit of hay that was too high for us to get up a couple of notches. That ain't somebody come out. I don't suppose he got more than a dollar a day. I worked for 35 cents a day from a neighbor planting onions. Little onion seeds. And then weeding the damn things. And then to help him harvest them and put them in sex. They got 35 cents a day. Now you put that in your pipe and smoke it. Right?

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did that money go to you or did it go to you?

segments.speaker: George Mckeever
segments.words: That was my money. You bet. Gosh, I ordered that my cow. Old King Midas himself. Now that was my money. It wasn't very much either because, you know, we had to do our own work. But when he needed help, I helped him. I knocked on my hands and knees. I thought my back would break. And those great big long rows. We had to thin those darn onions. You know, they come up little green devils. Thin them and hold them. And hold them all the way, keep the weeds out. And then help him harvest them. Put them in, got his sacks. 35 cents a day. And I tell these kids today, oh, you're crazy. You never did that. Well, that's a guy's truth. I didn't. And I can take you right out and show you the field today where we worked. Those old places right out there just two miles from here.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: When you were thinking about becoming a dentist, did was the, where you, did you feel it or know that there was a pretty good living in it to be a dentist or a doctor?

segments.speaker: George Mckeever
segments.words: I don't think that ever entered into my head. It was something. Those days you had to figure to know what you wanted to do. And then go ahead with it. And I don't think the money angle ever entered my noggin at all. Not for one minute… no.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: How was it for doctors and dentists and eagerly gays in these small towns? Was it a good living for them?

segments.speaker: George Mckeever
segments.words: I think better than average. You'd be amazed at how much people that didn't know your money would bring you in chickens, bring you in ham, bacon, sausage, eggs, give it to you. Because I'd be a good gentleman to let them pay when they could pay, you know. In those days we didn't have much money. Yes, it was a better than average. You know, we worked like the devil too long, didn't we… busy.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did you work full day every day?

segments.speaker: George Mckeever
segments.words: I always, my first patient was eight o 'clock. Every day in the week, Saturday. I never took a day off. Never did I ever take a day off until, from 1923 up to 19, in the sickness or something. I never took a day off in my life for a vacation, no. Until my girls graduated, the oldest one from the university. Then we had our first vacation. We went in every state in the union. And that was really something in those days.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Your first patient was an eight, and what was your last?

segments.speaker: George Mckeever
segments.words: Time for me to get in and eat my, we call it supper because it's in the farming country, and the ate supper. It's dinner, you know. If I was through with a patient and I had some lab work to do, I didn't until dinner was ready or supper. Then after that I went out and watered the yard. I watered half of it one night and dragged 600 feet of hose around. I watered the other half, and the next night I mow, and then start all over again watering. After dark, you might say, now it's out and you push a button and it's all underground and flake… no problem.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: When you think about, say, some of the other businessmen in town in those years, was there a lot of turnover in the businesses?

segments.speaker: George Mckeever
segments.words: No… no, they stayed right in that store until they died of old age and their son took over… right… the blacksmith, he did the same thing, and his son took over.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Was there an Alexander's store in this town? I saw an Alexander building here, though.

segments.speaker: George Mckeever
segments.words: I'll take it back… fred Beckwith… yes… alexander. You're right. But there was also an Alexander and Juliaetta. ... Same family. Same family… right.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Alexander and Juliaetta was Jewish, I understand.

segments.speaker: George Mckeever
segments.words: Did you ever hear of Evan Adams in Moscow? Yes. Now, Evan Adams and his wife was an Alexander, and quite a heavy lady. She came to me one day when I was through. My wife was sick for three years. Just about lost her head. Well, forget it. She was in Spokane a long time up there, and her mother came and helped me with the kids. And Mrs. Adams came to me when Paula was five years old. She says, listen, you send that girl to school. I want her. And so Paula started school when she was five years old. Ninety miles from here, from Grangeville. Now, tell me, I had Kamiah or Kooskia. That lady was calling from Kamiah right now. And she's one of the few that's on my list… lewiston… sometimes I think I had more patients from Lewiston than those darn dentists down there ever had in their offices… ever.

segments.speaker: George Mckeever
segments.words: You know, more patients.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: You know, speaking of Lewiston, it makes me think of that foster, Dr. Foster in Juliaetta. The old chiropractor, the old, uh, was he chiropractor? I've heard he was both. Could he have been both? No. Some people say chiropractor, some people say ... Yeah, but there is a little difference.

segments.speaker: George Mckeever
segments.words: Some people just call him a ... doctor. What do they... health... Oh, you know what I'm trying to tell you. They don't believe in medication. Oh, the naturopath. That's the word I was trying to think… yes… foster was that. More, I think, than anything else. He took off a million cancers off of people, or at least he claimed they were cancers. And he was of what we would call a naturopath, you know. Yes, you bet. And his sons had offices in... pardon me, in Clarkston.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did you know anything about whether he did what he claimed or what kind of setup he had there?

segments.speaker: George Mckeever
segments.words: You know, in those days, it's been a good many years ago, that if he said something, you either believed or you didn't believe it. I don't know what to believe. But he had a heck of a business going down in Juliaetta, you know. He had an enormous clientele, or whatever you want to call him, a group of patients or whatever. An endless row of them. They went down there and they moved in and they stayed there until they were well. And then go back home. Either that or died. I never knew the old gentleman. I was too young. But I knew his boys and they lived over in the head offices in Clarkson. In fact, I'd been to one. Just got hurt in the Navy a little bit. Jammed up and still got a bum hit from the darn thing. And I go to... Do you know Dr… nellie Scott? Moscow… right across from the Moscow Public Library. Just down this way from the common house. I believe twice a week, year after year after year, I go to that lady.

segments.speaker: George Mckeever
segments.words: Right… and I think that's one reason why I'm 80 years old and can still do a good day's work if I'm going to. In the Reader's Digest one time, there was quite an article there that told about that if anybody, whoever, don't make endeavors what his occupation was, that if he would take a chiropractic treatment every so often, he would be much better physically than if he didn't. Keeps you limber, keeps you old. Joints from getting stiff on your end. I don't know. When I go to Dr. Scott and we've known her, she's one year older than I am. And we've been on some oversea trips with that old gal. And she's pretty skookum old gal. One of the old schools. She doesn't believe in taking a million X-rays every time you come in with a pain in your watch mcconnell. She'll tell you where that pain is without the X-ray. And she'll give you that adjustment without the help of the X-ray. And I know, my gosh, you go in for yourselves first thing you do.

segments.speaker: George Mckeever
segments.words: I believe his name was McIntosh. At one time we had two papers here at Kennedy. And they consolidated. And I believe McIntosh was the... I think McIntosh was the editor of one of those papers. And he's the one that stayed. And then Ralph Nefer. And Ralph never sold out to McCreary's, a bitch and a Parker. And they sold out to... Gee, Bill Mann McCreary died. Bill died. His wife died of cancer. Both of them of cancer. And this little guy from Genesee is here now, Ralph. Now that would take you back to 1900 and..… fire times… sure, I can still see those old presses they had. And if they had burnt up, when things cooled off, the problem would be the kids prowling around.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Doesn't seem to me like the best living in a small little town being a printer.

segments.speaker: George Mckeever
segments.words: Those monkeys make money hand over fist. They get so many jobs out of town, job work… and McCreary's got..… oh, just..… you couldn't believe what old man McCreary would draw in here. Handy bills and pretty... I don't know why. That press was running practically all the time. Well, that's the thing. You keep that press running all the time down here.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: But if all you've got is that weekly pay for it, then you've got... Well, I wanted to ask you about why it is that most of the people who, let's say, came from here, became doctors, dentists, or professional people like lawyers, would leave. You have much money in YC, because I can't find them. They're all gone, you know?

segments.speaker: George Mckeever
segments.words: The most noted one that came from Kendrick and Ruby and I kept him when he went to high school here. We lived up in a school, had a two-story house, and this old farmer came in and asked us if we would make his boy in… and... sure… and it wasn't for just to accommodate him. We didn't have school buses. It was too far in for him to walk. He's one of the world's most noted cancer man today. Dwight Engel. Maybe you remember the name. He stayed with us in high school. And every time Dwight Engel comes to Kendrick, he spends a half a day with us in here.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: You decided to stay, not go someplace else… why was that?

segments.speaker: George Mckeever
segments.words: I just liked the ground, and I liked the people, and it was...

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: what, my class? My style?

segments.speaker: George Mckeever
segments.words: I don't know. It'll kill me to go to a big city and have an office. I don't like that. Hop up and down on the damn elevator, have to take your car out and drive 20 miles down to your office. No, that never did appeal to me. My girl was a medical pathologist in San Diego. She gets up and goes to work fighting traffic, four lanes. Coming in four lanes a goin', morning and night. No, that's not for me. That would kill me off with nothing flat… free on it… i had more damn fun out here with my garden, my flowers. Fishing up to the last two or three years... elk and deer. Now my patients bringing me in elk and deer steak, and I don't have to go.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did you ever seriously think about going someplace else?

segments.speaker: George Mckeever
segments.words: Never entered my head once, never. No. I had a guy here the other day. He wanted to lease my office. He says, you want to quit? I've half quit. I've only got 10 or 12 patients, that's all. He wanted to lease my office here. I didn't want nobody in my house. Nothing doin'. There's a place up town, five rooms up there. Come take a look at them. Anything that comes up, I'll help you get established. What was his name… richard George… ever hear the name? His wife teaches at the university. If you wanted to get an apartment and live in Troy, he'd come down here one day a week and go home. And I told him, I said, just shut my head. I don't think he'd make a living, that's just one day a week. You've got to be on the job every day in the week, or nearly every day in the week, you know. So, I've had five different guys come here, and their wives won't live in a small town. Six, six come. This is George, Guy George, Richard George. And he was here about two weeks ago. And now that the office has space, and I was telling you about the back of the drug store, he's got five good rooms up there. And he's going to have an empty in there. So this fellow, if you wanted to fly, he's out of luck now.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What do you think of that rivalry between Kendrick and Juliaetta? Was it a real rivalry?

segments.speaker: George Mckeever
segments.words: It really was 40 years ago, Red Hot. You darn right. I've seen more damn heights in these baseball games. You could check. I've seen, you just died in the nursing home up there just a few days ago. Seen her get so mad from Juliaetta, that'll throw a rock right through this guy's windshield of his car. Yeah, he's razzing her, you know, about, hey, dad, how healthy is she? She just died just a few days ago up there.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: The two towns are so close together for small towns.

segments.speaker: George Mckeever
segments.words: Do you know how come? No, tell me why. There was the guy that started Kendrick was the first engineer on the railroad train that came down here. That was his last name, Kendrick. He brought the first train into Kendrick, so they called the town Kendrick. It wasn't that name at first. They did change it for him. Juliaetta was established. And the guy that established Juliaetta, they had two daughters, Julia and Etta, and they named the town after those two girls. This other guy named these old, I won't mention the names because some of them are still here. They, their parents took up all the lots and they were going to sell them at an enormous price, you know. And the guy that came up here to start this town said, to hell with you. You come up here and start a town of his own. And he did. And that's how Kendrick got started.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: These lots were where? Right along?

segments.speaker: George Mckeever
segments.words: Right in, Juliaetta, right there. Right in the main drag, you know. He'd charge it to an exorbitant price. This guy wouldn't pay it. He said, to hell with you. I'm going up the creek here and I'll start a town of my own. And he did. In the first house built, I could show you right where the first house in this town was built. Bob Watts over there owns a land. I'm just having a lovely home, man. It's all down many years ago.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Who was that?

segments.speaker: George Mckeever
segments.words: The cabin.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Was that Kirby that started the town?

segments.speaker: George Mckeever
segments.words: Kirby and his wife. No, his daughter, Miss, married Louis Harris, who was our early, uh, druggist here. Louis Harris. Mrs. Louis Harris was Mrs. Lula Kirby. Miss Lula Kirby.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: And he started, he was the one that started the town.

segments.speaker: George Mckeever
segments.words: And he had that little long cabin there, where Bob Watts lives and across the street. He built the house that Marvin Long lives in now. That's one of the, what he called, historical. Yes, it's historical. Right. Besides, it's beautiful. Mm-hmm.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: I heard there was a, a woman who was a bartender or saloon keeper and either Juliaetta or Kent or, uh, can't remember her name, but I heard about that.

segments.speaker: George Mckeever
segments.words: You mean in the early days or now?

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: No, early days. Oh, now it's nothing unusual then. There's something big up in up the street right now. The envelope in is a woman run by a girl, you know, a lady.

segments.speaker: George Mckeever
segments.words: Patient of mine… i never heard of a woman being in any of the, we had three big saloons here. God, I can remember the old monogram saloon. The guy got drunk in a who-down and got on his horse. We had these old wooden sidewalks. And he moved that horse and told Gallop right on up from out of, right out of town, you know.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: On the sidewalk?

segments.speaker: George Mckeever
segments.words: Right on the sidewalk, you bet. Mm-hmm. I hear it. Kendrick, Ballroom. Yeah, Ballroom, yeah. Here's the old wooden sidewalk right here and that guy, here's where Dr. Moser lived. That was his old home. And he had his office right on the, open right on the, right on the sidewalk. And that guy rode his horse right up there a hundred miles an hour, you know, first little kids we thought it was because we jumped off and got out of the road. Drunk in a bad building and he drove his horse right up that sidewalk.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Did you, right on out of town? Did you used to see Indians in town when you were a kid?

segments.speaker: George Mckeever
segments.words: Always, always. And they went through, every fall they went huckleberrying. They'd come through here with a hack and a half a dozen Indian ponies loose following the hack. And they had whips sticking out in the back of the packs on those horses. And as they trotted the whips, paddled their horses and made them keep up with the rig. Hundreds of them, I see them go through here. And that's where my dad learned to talk to these people. Sold them their equipment to go back in the hills, either fishing, huckleberrying or in the fall with the big game hunting. Oh, he knew those old fat squads, my gosh. And outstanding, my dad and the people around Adam. When he was working in the store, you know.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Would you be scared of them?

segments.speaker: George Mckeever
segments.words: No. They didn't be scared of. Well, you know, some people were, especially in the farms.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: I've been living here all your life. No, we never were. You see the date on the little cow?

segments.speaker: George Mckeever
segments.words: 1835. That's as old as you are. A little bit more, a little bit older. Eclipse is in 1835. They had them those days, I guess. I'm surprised. I thought they must have been... More recently, yeah. Those things that started the moon program. Well, we had two banks, the Kendrick State Bank and the Farmer's Bank. And the Kendrick State Bank was on pretty shaky ground. And the state finally closed them up. And then the Farmer's Bank took them up, took them over. And they were backed by a bunch of pretty wealthy farmers up here. The guy that had the main part of it was a man by the name of Meyer. And he's dead now, but he was a millionaire over. And he owned the most stock in there. Well, when he dropped over dead in his farm yard up there on the hill, he answered down much about what would you call the holdings. He didn't have enough to pay his wife to pay the internal revenue. People made her sell the bank. And that's how the First Security got into Kendrick. He had so many holdings that she couldn't pay the... She had to sell something to get the money to pay the...

segments.speaker: George Mckeever
segments.words: What you'd call it? Inheritance tax or whatever. Yes. She absolutely had to sell the bank to get money to pay the government.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Where did he make his money from, just around here?

segments.speaker: George Mckeever
segments.words: 2000 acres, the best farmland in the country.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: Do you know how he ever got hold of so much land? The only person I heard that had land like that was Vollmer.

segments.speaker: George Mckeever
segments.words: Oh, Vollmer. He had the farmer's bank before the farmers bought it out. Look at that front page. 1849.

segments.speaker: Sam Schrager
segments.words: What about this guy? How did he get his land?

segments.speaker: George Mckeever
segments.words: Well, is that on? Well, I won't tell you. I don't know what you're going to do with this stuff.
